After 7 days, seedlings were transferred to pots containing a 2:1 Jiffy mix:vermiculite soil mixture. After approximately 21 days of growth, drought stress was applied by withholding water for 14 days. Survival rates were assessed 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

Seeds of EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants and wild-type controls were sown in 7 cm × 10 cm pots containing a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture and grown in a growth chamber. At the three-leaf stage, seedlings were exposed to 42 °C for 36 h and allowed to recover at 23 °C for 4 days. Seedling survival rates were calculated based on the number of individual plants with green, viable shoots. At least nine seedlings per genotype were analysed per assay, with three independent experiments. Maximum photochemical efficiency of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) was measured using a FluorPen FP110 fluorometer (PSI). Electrolyte leakage was determined using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-307F, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instruments). Relative electrolyte conductivity (%) was calculated as (C1 – C0)/(C2 – C0) × 100%, where C1 represents initial conductivity before boiling, C2 is the final conductivity after boiling and C0 is the conductivity of deionized water.

Sources indicate that wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants were cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Three-week-old seedlings were inoculated with Pst urediniospores and maintained in darkness at 12 °C and 100% relative humidity for 24 h, after which plants were returned to standard growth conditions. Disease phenotypes were evaluated following the development of stripe rust symptoms. Relative fungal biomass was quantified by qPCR analysis of the ratio of Pst-specific PstEF transcripts relative to that of the wheat reference gene, TaEF64, in CTAB-extracted genomic DNA.

In a recent development, for histological analyses, reactive oxygen species accumulation was visualized by staining infected leaves with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (1 mg ml−1). Stained samples were examined using a BX-51 microscope (Olympus). Stomata associated with haustorial mother-cell formation were defined as successful infection sites, and the 3,3′-diaminobenzidine-stained area at each site was quantified using CellSens Entry software (Olympus). At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point. Fungal infection structures were visualized by WGA–Alexa Fluor 488 staining (20 μg ml−1; Amresco) following tissue clearing and alkali treatment. Samples were mounted in 50% glycerol and examined using an Olympus BX-53 fluorescence microscope equipped with a GFP filter set. Substomatal vesicles, infection hyphae and other fungal structures were observed, and hyphal length and fungal colonization area were quantified using CellSens Entry software. At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point.

Wheat drought resistance at the maturity stage was evaluated under full-irrigation (that is, control) and water-limited conditions in the field. Each plot measured 5 m × 2 m and consisted of 25 rows, with 20-cm spacing between rows and 10 cm between plants. Control plots were irrigated regularly throughout the entire growing season, and water-limited plots were isolated using a 1.5-m-deep underground waterproof barrier and covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation. After the initial irrigation at sowing, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume applied to the well-watered plots for the remainder of the season.

It has been revealed that photosynthetic parameters of wheat were recorded with a LI-6400XT portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR) at four Zadoks growth stages from tillering (Z25) to milk development (Z75). Net photosynthesis rate (Pn), transpiration rate (Tr), stomatal conductance (Gs) and instantaneous water use efficiency (calculated as Pn/Tr) were measured from at least 15 plants per line. Light-response and CO2-response curves were fitted using the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry model to estimate maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) and maximum electron transport rate (Jmax). Chlorophyll fluorescence (Fv/Fm) and SPAD values were measured using a hand-held chlorophyll-fluorescence measurement instrument (FluorPen FP 110, FluorCam) and chlorophyll meter (SPAD-502, Konica Minolta), respectively. Leaf area of the main tiller was measured using a leaf-area meter (Yaxin-1242, Dianjiang Technology). Agronomic traits, including plant height, spike number, spike length, spikelet number, grain number per spike, grain length, grain width, 1,000-grain weight, yield per plant, biomass and harvest index were measured from 50–100 plants per line. Grains were oven-dried at 37 °C before yield quantification.

Rice agronomic traits were evaluated in the field at maturity. Seeds were sown in a seedling nursery and transplanted into the field at 25 days after sowing. A wide–narrow row-planting pattern was adopted in the field, with 5 rows × 10 plants per plot. Each line was randomly assigned to three plots (that is, three biological replicates). Water-limited plots were covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation, and drought stress was initiated at booting stage by withholding irrigation and opening drainage valves to remove standing water. Drought treatment was terminated and followed by a rewatering recovery phase once either the experimental or control plants showed irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms that persisted for 5 consecutive days. At maturity, each plant was harvested individually. Traits assessed included plant height, grain size, 1,000-grain weight and grain yield per plant.

Maize field trials were conducted at the three abovementioned locations under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions. Drought treatment was applied through artificial irrigation control using a drip irrigation system equipped with underground Watermark 200SS sensors to monitor and maintain soil water potential. Each treatment included four replicate plots (2.6 m wide; 0.4 m row spacing), with four rows per line. Agronomic traits, including plant height, grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight, were measured following open pollination.

Wheat lodging resistance was evaluated using the second basal internode of the main tiller. Stem breaking strength was measured at 10 days after anthesis using a plant stem strength tester (IN-JG2, Shandong Holder Electronic Technology). Stem diameter was measured on the same internode using a digital caliper. Each stem was measured three times, and 20 biological replicates were analysed for each genotype.

According to recent reports, for stem histology, the middle region of the peduncle internode was collected at 15 days post-anthesis and fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and clearing in xylene, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections (6–8 μm) were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems) and subjected to safranin–fast green double staining. In brief, sections were stained with safranin, differentiated in 90% ethanol, counterstained with fast green, cleared in a 1:1 (v/v) xylene–ethanol mixture and mounted. Panoramic images were acquired using SlideViewer software (v2.9.0), and stem diameter, vascular bundle number and mechanical tissue thickness were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

For seedling-stage stress experiments, germinated wheat seedlings were grown in 7 cm × 7 cm × 10 cm pots with Hoagland’s modified nutrient solution for 3 days under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Subsequently, the control group was continuously cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution, whereas the drought-stress group was cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution containing 20% (w/v) PEG6000. Seedlings in both groups were grown for 3–4 weeks, with the culture solution replaced every 3 days, after which root parameters were scored. The root system of each seedling was excised, lateral roots were separated from nodes, evenly spread in a transparent plastic tray with 0.5 cm of deionized water, and intertwined fine lateral branches were gently separated with forceps to avoid overlap. Primary root length, root fresh weight and root dry weight were measured manually.

Wheat plants were grown in PVC columns (150 cm × 15 cm) filled with soil under well-watered and water-limited (water supply terminated at the jointing stage) conditions, with one plant per column. When wheat reached the grain-filling stage, the soil and root system were carefully removed from the columns. Roots were rinsed with running water to remove adhering soil and impurities, then excised from shoots. Root length was measured immediately after cleaning. Subsequently, roots were placed in paper envelopes and dried in a forced-air drying oven at 65 °C for 7 days, after which root dry weight was determined.

Industry observers note that water loss assays were performed on 4-week-old wheat seedlings as previously described25. Fully expanded third leaves were excised and immediately weighed to record their initial fresh weight (FW0). Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper under ambient room conditions (22–25 °C, 40–60% relative humidity, with light exposure) without covering. Fresh weight (FWt) was recorded at regular intervals. Water loss was expressed as a percentage of the initial fresh weight using the formula: Water loss rate (%) = [(FW0 − FWt)/FW0] × 100. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Water loss assays on Arabidopsis were carried out as previously described65. In brief, fully expanded rosette leaves from 3-week-old plants were detached at the same time of day to minimize circadian effects. The initial fresh weight (FW0) was recorded immediately using a precision analytical balance. Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper in a controlled environment (22 °C, 50–60% relative humidity, no direct airflow). Fresh weights (FWt) were measured at specified time intervals, typically every 30 or 60 min for 6 h. Water loss rate was calculated using the same formula as for wheat. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Industry observers note that infrared thermography was performed on 4-week-old greenhouse-grown seedlings that were subjected to 15 days of water withholding, during which soil water content was maintained at approximately 50% of well-watered capacity. Leaf surface temperatures under different treatments were recorded using a FLIR A655sc infrared camera (Teledyne FLIR). Thermal images were analysed using FLIR ResearchIR Max (v4.40) to quantify temperature differences and assess drought-induced physiological responses.

It has been revealed that to evaluate photosynthesis-related changes, multispectral imaging was conducted using the PhenoBox live-plant multispectral imaging analysis system (LemnaTec GmbH). Five-leaf-stage wheat seedlings were individually cultivated in plots filled with nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture under controlled growth-chamber conditions. Imaging was performed under three distinct soil-moisture regimes, including well watered (soil water content maintained at approximately 90%), mild drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 50%) and severe drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 30%). Four surface multispectral images were captured for each plant. Standardized imaging protocols were applied to ensure consistent lighting and sensor calibration. Two spectral values, normalized water index and normalized difference vegetation index, were used to assess plant water status and physiological responses under drought stress: normalized water index = (R970 – R850)/(R970 + R850) and normalized difference vegetation index = (R800 – R670)/(R800 + R670), with R representing reflectance and numbers referring to wavelength (nm).

Sources indicate that for chlorophyll fluorescence measurements, imaging was performed using the live-plant imaging system CV-200 produced by Beijing Feizhi Technology and controlled by CropVision_Controller_v2 software. Fluorescence images were captured under stable-lighting conditions at the same time points used for multispectral imaging. The effective ΦPSII was automatically extracted using the software and was used to evaluate photosynthetic performance and drought-stress responses in wheat seedlings across the different water treatments.

Sources indicate that stomatal density measurements were performed following a published protocol66. To determine stomatal density in wheat, the middle region of the abaxial surface of the fully expanded second leaf of seedlings was selected for analysis. The abaxial epidermis was carefully adhered to a piece of transparent adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll tissue were then gently scraped off using a razor blade. The tape carrying the intact abaxial epidermal cells was subsequently mounted on a standard microscope slide (75 mm × 25 mm) for microscopic observation. A minimum of ten slides were prepared for each wheat line. Stomata were observed and photographed using compound microscope (Olympus IX71) under a ×10 objective lens, and stomatal density was calculated as the number of stomata per unit area of the field of view.

For Arabidopsis, fully expanded and healthy functional leaves (typically the fifth or sixth true leaf) were selected. The abaxial surface of each leaf was gently pressed onto clear adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll were carefully removed using a razor blade, leaving the lower epidermis adhered to the tape. The tape carrying the epidermal imprint was then mounted smoothly onto a standard glass slide (75 mm × 25 mm), avoiding air bubbles. At least ten slides were prepared per line for analysis.

Stomatal aperture measurements in wheat and Arabidopsis were determined following established protocols65. For wheat, a fully expanded second leaf was excised and incubated in stomatal opening buffer containing 0.05 M KNO3, 10 mM MES and 50 μM CaCl2 (pH 6.15) under light conditions (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1, 25 °C) for 1.5 h or in darkness for 1 h. Leaves were then exposed to drought treatment under ambient air for 10 min, followed by incubation in continuous light, continuous dark or a light-to-dark transition for 30 min. The abaxial surface was carefully blot dried and adhered to transparent tape, and the adaxial epidermis and mesophyll cells were gently removed using a razor blade. The exposed abaxial epidermal layer on the tape was then mounted on a microscope slide for imaging. For Arabidopsis, the fifth or sixth rosette leaves were harvested and incubated in MES buffer (10 mM MES-KOH, pH 6.15, 10 mM KCl and 50 μM CaCl2) in a light incubator for 2.5 h to induce stomatal opening. The leaves were subsequently transferred to MES buffer containing 20% w/v PEG6000 and incubated for 2 h. Epidermal strips were prepared and imaged using a compound microscope (Olympus IX71). Stomatal aperture was defined as the width of the pore between the two guard cells, and the stomatal aperture ratio (width:length) was measured using ImageJ (v1.8.0). Data for each ecotype were collected from a minimum of 100 stomata.

Wheat seedlings were grown under controlled conditions until the three-leaf stage. Once soil moisture content declined below 30%, leaf samples were collected at designated intervals. Each genotype comprised three biological replicates, with each sample weighing no less than 1.5 g. Samples were placed in dry envelopes and dried in a constant-temperature forced-air oven at 60 °C until completely desiccated. The dried tissue was then ground into a fine powder for carbon isotope analysis using the stable-isotope ratio mass spectrometry method. Ground samples were treated with 4 mol dm−3 HCl for 24 h, then washed with deionized water until neutral, dried, ground and sieved through a 60-mesh screen. Approximately 0.4 mg of the solid sample was accurately weighed, placed into a tin cup and hermetically sealed, and placed in a 96-well plate. Isotopic measurements were conducted using a Flash 1112 Elemental Analyzer coupled to a Delta V Plus Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan). The carbon isotope ratio (δ13C) was calculated relative to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) international standard using the formula: δ13C (‰) = [(Rsample/RVPDB) – 1] × 1,000, where R is the ratio of 13C to 12C. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Industry observers note that uniform wheat seeds were germinated at room temperature for 3 days and subsequently grown in half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution for 1 week. Seedlings were then subjected to either control conditions or drought stress induced by 15% (w/v) PEG6000. After 10 days of treatment, leaf and root tissues were harvested, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Three independent biological replicates were collected for each treatment. Hormone quantification was performed by Metware Biotechnology using an AB Sciex QTRAP 6500 LC–MS/MS system.

Wheat seeds were sown side by side in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. Seedlings were cultured under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature and 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days (three-leaf stage). Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until leaf wilting was observed. Leaves were collected from at least three individual plants under well-watered and drought-stressed conditions. The activity of RuBisCO, along with the contents of chlorophyll, soluble sugars, sucrose, glucose and starch were measured using commercial assay kits all obtained from Solarbio: BC0445 for RuBisCO activity, BC0995 for chlorophyll, BC2460 for sucrose, BC0030 for soluble sugars, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch, all following the manufacturer’s instructions. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Industry observers note that to evaluate wheat grain development and filling dynamics, main tiller spikes were tagged before anthesis. Under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, grains from the six central spikelets of each tagged spike were sampled at 5-day intervals from anthesis to physiological maturity, with a minimum of nine spikes collected per genotype per time point. Grain length, width and thickness were measured in 60–100 grains with a digital caliper (0.01-mm resolution); fresh weight was determined for 100-grain samples. Dry weight was obtained by drying samples at 80 °C to a constant weight following a 30-min pre-treatment at 105 °C. The mean grain-filling rate was calculated as the final grain dry weight divided by the grain-filling duration, expressed as mg per grain per day.

In a recent development, flag leaf sheaths and developing grains were harvested at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 days after flowering. Soluble sugars (sucrose, fructose and glucose) and starch contents were quantified using commercial assay kits from Solarbio (BC2460 for sucrose, BC6360 for fructose, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch). Enzymatic activity assays were conducted using kits for sucrose synthase (SUS; BC0585), cell-wall invertase (CWI; BC4325) and ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (AGPase; BC0435) following the manufacturer’s protocols. All assays were performed with at least three independent biological replicates.

Recent findings suggest that for grain histology, developing grains were collected from central spikelets at 15 days after flowering, then fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution (G2355, Solarbio) at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and xylene clearing, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections of 6–8 μm thickness were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems). For histological analysis, sections were stained with toluidine blue, whereas starch granules were visualized using periodic acid–Schiff reagent. Images were acquired using SlideViewer panoramic scanning software (v2.9.0). Grain cell size, cell number and starch granule number were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

It has been revealed that total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 μg of DNase-treated RNA using the HiScript reverse transcription kit (R223-01, Vazyme). RT–qPCR was performed in a 20-μl reaction volume containing 1.4 μl cDNA (pre-diluted to a concentration of 200 ng μl−1), 0.4 μM primers and 10 μl of SYBR Green Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme), using a CFX96 real-time PCR system (Bio-Rad). Gene-expression levels were calculated using the \({2}^{-\Delta \Delta {{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{T}}}}\) method67 with TaActin1 (TraesCS1B01G283900) serving as the reference gene for normalization. Primer sequences used for RT–qPCR are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

In a recent development, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Δhog1 mutant, which is sensitive to osmotic stress and lacks a functional copy of a gene encoding a high osmolarity glycerol 1 protein kinase (HOG1)68, was used to assess the drought-resistance function of TFIIAγ proteins. Coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were amplified via PCR using primers with flanking attB sites. These fragments were first cloned into the pDONR221 entry vector (Invitrogen) via BP recombination using the Gateway cloning system and subsequently transferred into the pGAD426 destination vector (Addgene) through an LR (attL and attR) recombination reaction. Recombinant plasmids were transformed into Δhog1 cells using the Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation Kit (Zymo Research). Transformed strains were selected on synthetic dropout medium lacking uracil (SD−Ura). The pGAD426-GUS plasmid was used as a control.

Industry observers note that for stress-tolerance assays, 10 μl of yeast culture (OD600 nm = 0.6) was spotted onto SD−Ura solid medium supplemented with 0.75 M sorbitol and incubated at 28 °C for 3 days. Growth in SD−Ura liquid medium containing 0.75 M sorbitol was monitored by measuring OD600 nm at 24-h intervals.

The full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ (excluding translational stop codons) were cloned in-frame into the N-terminal region of the pJIT163-GFP expression vectors64, both driven by the CaMV 35S promoter. The resulting fusion constructs were introduced into wheat protoplasts (pJIT163-TFIIAγ-GFP). Transformed wheat protoplasts were incubated for 16 h to permit transient expression. GFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength range of 500–530 nm. Nuclei were labelled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), and fluorescence signal was verified to originate solely from intact fusion proteins via anti-GFP western blot.

Recent findings suggest that fluorescence imaging was conducted in wheat protoplasts and N. benthamiana epidermal cells transiently expressing EpTFIIAγ–GFP. To induce drought-stress-related or osmotic stress-related cellular responses, cells were treated with 10% (w/v) PEG8000, 1.5 M sorbitol, 50 μM ABA or 250 mM NaCl as indicated. Imaging was performed with an FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus). GFP fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and emission was captured at 491–535 nm. Image acquisition and processing were performed using FV31S-SW software.

Sources indicate that molecular dynamics of EpTFIIAγ–GFP condensates were characterized through FRAP assays. Selected condensates were photobleached using a 488-nm laser, and fluorescence recovery was monitored by timelapse imaging. Recovery curves were normalized to both pre-bleach intensity and the fluorescence of adjacent unbleached regions to correct for background photobleaching; data were analysed with FV31S-SW software. Molecular mobility of EpTFIIAγ and the IDR deletion variant was assessed by FCS analysis in wheat protoplasts. Autocorrelation curves were acquired from multiple cells and fitted to appropriate diffusion models using CorTector NanoX FCS software to obtain diffusion coefficients and molecular concentrations.

It has been revealed that to identify proteins that can potentially physically interact with EpTFIIAγ, a yeast two-hybrid screen was performed. The full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector and served as the bait construct, fused to the binding domain of GAL4. The resulting pGBKT7-EpTFIIAγ plasmid was co-transformed with a pGADT7-based cDNA library (from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings) into S. cerevisiae strain AH109 using the lithium acetate method, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Clontech). Positive clones were selected on selective dropout media, and candidate-interacting proteins were identified by PCR amplification and subsequent DNA sequencing.

To validate putative physical interactions between EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ with candidate partners, the coding sequences lacking translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were individually cloned into the pGADT7 vector to form prey constructs. The coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were used as bait in the pGBKT7 vector. Bait and prey constructs were co-transformed into S. cerevisiae AH109 using the lithium-acetate method. Protein–protein interactions were assessed by spotting serial tenfold dilutions of co-transformed yeast cultures onto SD/–Trp–Leu and SD/–Trp–Leu–His–Ade selective media.

Recent findings suggest that to perform luciferase-complementation imaging assays, the coding sequences of TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaAKS1, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were cloned upstream of the nLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-nLUC vector, whereas EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned downstream of the cLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-cLUC vector. These constructs were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and cultured overnight. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.6 in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 150 μM acetosyringone and 10 mM MES, pH 5.6). Equal volumes of Agrobacteria carrying pairs of nLUC and cLUC constructs of interest and controls were co-infiltrated into 4-week-old N. benthamiana leaves. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, 150 μg ml−1 D-luciferin potassium salt (ST196, Beyotime) was sprayed onto the abaxial surface of tobacco leaves, followed by a 3-min dark reaction. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using a PlantView100 multispectral dynamic fluorescence microscope system (BLT Photon Technology).

Recent findings suggest that for bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ lacking the translational stop codon was amplified and cloned into the cYFP vector pSm35s-cYFP (BioRun), whereas the coding sequences lacking the translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 were amplified and cloned into the nYFP vector pSm35s-nYFP (BioRun). The resulting constructs were introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants. The infiltration buffer contained 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, adjusted to pH 5.6. The bacterial suspension was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.4 before infiltration. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 514 nm and an emission wavelength range of 525–555 nm.

The same constructs were transformed into wheat protoplasts, which were incubated for 20 h to allow transient expression. YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus), with nuclei labelled using DAPI. Total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were obtained for SDS–PAGE and western blotting. Western blotting (described below) was performed using the primary antibody anti-GFP tag mouse monoclonal antibody (1:1,000; A02020, Abbkine), followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

It has been revealed that full-length cDNAs of EpTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46 were amplified by PCR and cloned into the pMAL-c5X vector (for MBP tagging), pET32a (Novagen; for His or HA tagging) or the pGEX4T-1 vector (Merck; for GST-tagged expression) using the ClonExpress II One-Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme) following the manufacturers’ instructions and lacking the respective translational start or stop codons as required. The resulting recombinant plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta and cultured in LB medium supplemented with ampicillin at 37 °C. When the culture reached OD600 nm of 0.4–0.6, protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation at 16 °C for 14–16 h. The expressed proteins and corresponding controls were subsequently purified using the GST-tag Protein Purification Kit (P2253, Beyotime), anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) or Dextrin beads 6FF (SA026100, Smart-Lifesciences) according to the respective manufacturer’s protocols. The proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected with anti-HA (AH158-IgG1, Beyotime), anti-GST (AM926, Beyotime) and anti-MBP (66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group) antibodies, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that MBP-tagged EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were individually incubated with GST, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaARF6, HA–TaVOZ1, GST–TaTFIIAαβ or GST–AtTFIIAαβ at 4 °C for 3 h. Protein complexes were immunoprecipitated using BeyoGold GST-tag purification resin (P2253, Beyotime) or anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) at 4 °C for 4 h. After incubation, complexes were collected by centrifugation at 300g for 5 min, followed by five washes with phosphate-buffered saline. Proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected by western blotting (described below) using anti-GST antibody (1:1,000 dilution; AM926, Beyotime), anti-HA antibody (1:1,000 dilution, AF2305, Beyotime) and anti-MBP antibody (1:1,000 dilution; 66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group), and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) or goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies (diluted 1:1,000; A0216 and A0208, respectively, Beyotime).

Sources indicate that for co-immunoprecipitation assays, fusion constructs including EpTFIIAγ–GFP, TaAKS1–GFP, TaARF6–mCherry, TaWRKY46–mCherry, EpTFIIAγ–mCherry and TaVOZ1–GFP were prepared in pCAMBIA1302 and pICH86988 vectors, respectively. Combinations of these constructs were co-transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101, which was subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of N. benthamiana in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH of 5.6). After 48 h of transient expression, total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P1015, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were incubated with GFP-Trap beads (GTA-20, ChromoTek) at 4 °C for 3 h with gentle rotation. Corresponding protein complexes were obtained after a series of washing steps and elution steps. Input and eluted proteins were then resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Western blotting was performed using primary antibodies to GFP (1:2,000; AE012, Abclonal) or mCherry (1:1,000; ABM40125, Abbkine), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

EpTFIIAγ and SEUSS69 were cloned into the pET-15b expression vector (for His tagging) and heterologously expressed in E. coli Rosetta cells. The recombinant proteins were purified using NTA-Ni magnetic agarose beads with the His-Tag Protein Purification Kit (P2247S, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For phase-separation assays, purified proteins were diluted to 10 μM in phase-separation buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM dithiothreitol). 10% PEG8000 was included as a molecular crowding agent to promote condensate formation. Samples were gently mixed and equilibrated at room temperature before imaging. Condensates were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) equipped with a ×60 oil-immersion objective (NA = 1.42) and images were processed using FV31S-SW software.

Protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (PA115-02, Tiangen Biotech). SDS–PAGE was performed with a PAGE Gel Fast Preparation Kit (EpiZyme). Protein samples (obtained from either prokaryotic expression, in vitro and in planta validation) were mixed with 5× SDS loading buffer at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. Ten micrograms of protein sample and 5 μl of 10–180 kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) were loaded onto gels. Electrophoresis was run at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. For wet transfer, the gel, 0.45-μm PVDF membrane and filter papers were soaked in transfer buffer (PS109, EpiZyme) for 15 min to equilibrate. A transfer stack was assembled, and transfer was conducted at a constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C. Post-transfer, the PVDF membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in transfer buffer; PS109, EpiZyme) on a shaker at room temperature for 2 h. The membrane was then incubated with primary antibody (1:1,000 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk, adjusted per antibody instructions) on a shaker at 4 °C overnight. After three washes with TBST (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20), the membrane was incubated with 1:1,000 HRP-labelled secondary antibody (diluted in 5% w/v non-fat milk) at room temperature for 1.5 h. The membrane was washed three times with TBST and once with TBS for 5 min. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL substrate (34098CN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after 2 min of dark incubation, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system.

Sources indicate that transgenic wheat, rice, maize and Arabidopsis plants, along with non-transgenic controls, were used for the assay for EpTFIIAγ abundance. The anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody was generated by Genecreate via rabbit immunization with EpTFIIAγ-specific short polypeptides, and its specificity was verified by western blotting. Seedlings of rice, maize and wheat were grown to the three-leaf stage under the aforementioned culture conditions; Arabidopsis seedlings were grown for 2 weeks. For each plant, 2 g of leaves were weighed, swiftly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into powder in a pre-cooled mortar. The powder was transferred to a pre-cooled 50-ml centrifuge tube, and 5 ml of plant RIPA lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (50×; P1055, Beyotime) was added. After resuspension, the mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, then centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent experiments. Protein concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) method. A total of 15–20 μg of protein was mixed with 5× SDS–PAGE sample loading buffer (P0015, Beyotime) at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. SDS–PAGE was performed with a 12% separating gel: electrophoresis at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. A 10–180-kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) was used as a reference. Proteins were transferred to a 0.45-μm PVDF membrane by wet transfer (constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C for 90 min). The membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in TBST) at room temperature for 2 h, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody (1:500 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk). After three washes with TBST, the membrane was incubated with HRP-labelled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (A0208, Beyotime) at 1:5,000 dilution for 1 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membrane was developed with ECL chemiluminescent substrate, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system. The target protein expression level was analysed based on the presence of the target band. Actin was used as a loading control, detected with an anti-actin antibody (AA128, Beyotime) and HRP-labelled goat anti-mouse secondary antibody (A0216, Beyotime).

In a recent development, total protein was extracted from seedling leaves using plant protein extraction buffer (AS08300, Agrisera). Equal amounts of protein (10 μg) were resolved by 12.5% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Amersham, GE Healthcare). Membranes were probed with primary antibodies to Cyt b6 (AS184069, Agrisera), PsbA (AS05084, Agrisera), PsbD (AS06146, Agrisera), AtpB (AS05085, Agrisera), RbcL (AS03037, Agrisera), RbcS (AS07259, Agrisera), Lhca2 (AS01006, Agrisera) and Lhcb2 (AS01003, Agrisera) at the recommended dilutions, followed by incubation with a goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:10,000; AS09602, Agrisera). Actin (AA128, Beyotime) served as the loading control, and protein signals were visualized using the standard chemiluminescence detection described above.

Three-leaf-stage seedling leaves of transgenic wheat expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder background were collected and used for ChIP as previously described70. In brief, 2 g of plant tissue was washed twice with cold phosphate-buffered saline buffer and crosslinked with 1% v/v formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. The crosslinking was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 125 mM. Samples were then lysed in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 1% w/v SDS and protease inhibitor cocktail. Chromatin was extracted on ice and sonicated to obtain soluble, sheared fragments with an average DNA length of 200–500 bp. A 20-μl aliquot was reserved as the input control and stored at –20 °C, whereas 100 μl of the sheared chromatin was used for immunoprecipitation with 10 μg of anti-HA antibody (ChIP grade, ab9110, Abcam) overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, 30 μl of protein A/G magnetic beads was added, followed by incubation for 3 h. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 50 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% v/v Triton X-100 and 0.1% w/v SDS), twice with high-salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 250 mM LiCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% v/v NP-40 and 1% w/v deoxycholic acid), and twice with TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 1 mM EDTA). Chromatin was eluted in 300 μl of elution buffer (100 mM NaHCO3 and 1% w/v SDS), treated with RNase A (8 μg ml−1) at 65 °C for 6 h, followed by proteinase K (345 μg ml−1) digestion overnight at 45 °C. Immunoprecipitated DNA was then used to prepare sequencing libraries using the NEXTFLEX ChIP–seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NOVA-5143-02, Bioo Scientific) and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using a paired-end 150-bp strategy.

Low-quality sequencing reads were filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome (IWGSC RefSeq v1.1) using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72. SAMtools (v1.3.1)73 was used to remove PCR duplicates from the aligned data. MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 was used for peak calling using default parameters (bandwidth = 300 bp; model fold = 5, 50; q value = 0.05). Each peak was assigned to the gene for the TSS of which was closest to the peak midpoint. Motif analysis within the peaks was conducted using HOMER (v3)75 with default settings and a maximum motif length of 12 bp. Gene Ontology functional enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package in R76. Statistical significance was determined using a hypergeometric test with a P value threshold of 0.05.

To validate ChIP–seq results, ChIP–qPCR was performed. One microlitre of purified ChIP DNA was used as template in a 20-μl qPCR containing SYBR Green Master Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme). Amplification was carried out using a Bio-Rad CFX96 real-time PCR system. Primers were designed to amplify genomic regions containing predicted binding sites based on ChIP–seq results. Each qPCR was conducted in four times. Enrichment values were calculated as mean ± s.d. from three biological replicates and are presented. Non-specific IgG and primers targeting intergenic regions were included as negative controls. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

Total RNA was extracted from leaves of wild-type Fielder and two EpTFIIAγ–HA transgenic lines (TL4 and TL7) using TRIzol reagent (15596026, Invitrogen). Genomic DNA was removed by DNase I treatment following extraction. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a Nanodrop OneC Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by examining the A260:A280 ratio. RNA integrity was confirmed through 1.5% w/v agarose gel electrophoresis and quantified using a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer with the Qubit RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Q10210, Life Technologies). For library construction, 2 μg of total RNA was used to prepare strand-specific RNA-seq libraries with the KC Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (DR08402, Wuhan Seqhealth), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were enriched for fragments ranging from 200 to 500 bp, quantified and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform using paired-end reads.

Raw sequencing reads were quality filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71 to remove adapter sequences and low-quality reads. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome IWGSC RefSeq (v1.1) using GEM (v2.5)77. PCR duplicates were removed, and gene expression levels were quantified using DESeq2 (ref. 78). DEGs were identified using a threshold of |log2 (fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. Gene Ontology classification and enrichment analysis of DEGs were conducted using the clusterProfiler package76, identifying statistically significantly enriched terms among upregulated and downregulated genes.

Recent findings suggest that paired-end CUT&Tag79 reads were quality filtered with fastp80 and aligned to the wheat cv. Fielder reference genome using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72 in end-to-end, very-sensitive mode. Reads with mapping quality < 20 were removed, and duplicate reads were removed after processing with samtools fixmate and samtools markdup73. Genome-wide RPKM-normalized bigWig tracks were generated with deepTools bamCoverage, and signal enrichment around genes and TSSs was visualized using computeMatrix and plotHeatmap81. Peaks were called for each replicate with MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 using matched IgG/input controls. Reproducible peaks between biological replicates were identified using IDR82 and used as consensus peaks. Consensus peaks were annotated against the Fielder genome annotation83. Promoter-associated target genes were defined at the peak–gene pair level: a gene was retained only when its own signed distance from the peak to the TSS satisfied distance to TSS ≤ 3 kb. Motif enrichment was performed on promoter peak regions using HOMER75 with sequence extraction and shuffled genomic background generation performed using BEDTools84.

EMSA was performed using the Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (GS009, Beyotime Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Biotin-labelled DNA probes containing putative binding motifs were synthesized by Sangon Biotech and used at a final concentration of 0.05 μM per reaction. Each 20-μl binding reaction contained 4 μl of 5× EMSA/gel-shift binding buffer, 1 μg of recombinant protein (MBP tagged or GST tagged) and the biotin-labelled probe. Reactions were incubated at 23 °C for 30 min, then separated on a native 8% polyacrylamide gel in 0.5× TBE buffer (R0223, Beyontime) at 100 V for 1 h. DNA–protein complexes were transferred onto a nylon membrane (FFN10, Beyontime) and crosslinked by UV. Detection of biotin-labelled DNA was performed using a streptavidin–HRP conjugate and chemiluminescent substrate according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Negative controls included using MBP or GST. Washing and visualization were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

In a recent development, to assess transcriptional regulation mediated by EpTFIIAγ, 1.5-kb promoter regions of selected target genes were cloned into the pGreenII-0800-LUC vector to produce reporter constructs, whereas the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector to produce an effector construct25. Empty pGreenII-0800-LUC and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. LUC and REN activities were subsequently measured using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime), and relative luciferase activity was calculated as the ratio of LUC-to-REN activity.

To investigate the effect of EpTFIIAγ on the transcriptional activity of its assayed interacting proteins (TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46), the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pCAMBIA1302 vector, whereas the coding sequences of the transcription factors were cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector. Promoter regions (1.5 kb) of downstream target genes (TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1) were cloned into pGreenII-0800-LUC to generate reporter constructs. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. Luciferase activities were measured as described above, and relative transcriptional activity was determined by calculating the LUC:REN ratio. Empty pCAMBIA1302 and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. All experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates.

Fungal and plant TFIIAγ candidates were retrieved from the JGI MycoCosm portal85 and the OneKP project86, respectively. Protein-level similarity searches were conducted using EpTFIIAγ and representative TFIIAγ proteins as queries. Partial fragments and sequences with abnormal lengths (outside 70–150 amino acids) were removed. Redundant identical sequences from the same species were collapsed, but distinct isoforms passing the filtering criteria were retained. Ultimately, 3,183 fungal and 1,245 Viridiplantae sequences were included, resulting in a final dataset of 4,428 TFIIAγ proteins (Supplementary Table 7).

Filtered protein sequences were aligned with MAFFT (v7.525)87 using the automatic strategy selection mode. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference was performed with IQ-TREE (v3.0.1)88. The best-fitting amino acid substitution model was selected with ModelFinder, and branch support was estimated using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates and 1,000 Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood ratio test replicates. The resulting tree was visualized as a circular phylogeny using custom Python scripts with Biopython (v1.84) and Matplotlib (v3.10.8).

Sources indicate that protein structure prediction for TFIIAγ was conducted using AlphaFold3 (ref. 89) for orthologues from E. pusillum (EPUS02736), wheat (TraesCS1D02G024600), rice (LOC_Os01g73890), maize (Zm00001eb356100) and Arabidopsis (AT4G24440) with default parameters, and the resulting models were visualized using PyMOL (v3.1.0).

Statistical tests were conducted using two-tailed Student’s t-tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, one-way ANOVA, and Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA in GraphPad Prism (v9.5.0). Differences were considered statistically significant at *P < 0.05 or **P < 0.01. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. from at least three independent biological replicates or independent experiments unless otherwise specified in legends.

J.W., Z.K. and H.M. conceived the original idea and designed the early experiments. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the major experimental work. Specifically, L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.W., P.J., Y.H., D.T., S.Y., Q.W., S.T., Z.S., L.S., M.Y., T.X., Y.L., S.Z., P.Z., W.F., J.H., J.Z. and G.Z. contributed to plant cultivation and phenotypic characterization under controlled and field conditions, including stress-resistance phenotyping, agronomic trait assessment, grain-filling analysis and physiological measurements. X.H. generated the transgenic plants. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.T., Z.S., L.S. and J.H. conducted the microscopy and imaging analyses. F.L., H.Z., B.L., C.W., D.T. and Q.W. performed the biochemical and protein-related experiments. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.W., S.W., S.L. and D.T. conducted the molecular and transcriptional regulation assays. B.C., Z.Q. and Y.W. performed the genomic, transcriptomic and computational analyses. L.D. and Z.Q. conducted the phylogenetic analysis and protein structure prediction. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the statistical analyses and data quantification. H.M. and L.D. wrote the manuscript with input from X.Q., J.W. and Z.K. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.

Fielder (WT) and three transgenic lines overexpressing TaTFIIAγ. Photographs were taken before and after the drought treatment followed by a 3-d period of re-watering. Scale bars, 2 cm. Fielder (WT) and transgenic EpTFIIAγ seedlings germinated on nutrient solution (control) and 20% PEG for 7 d. Scale bar, 2 cm. Fielder and transgenic lines grown in control nutrient solution and 20% PEG for 14 d. Scale bars, 5 cm. (l–o) Root length (l), shoot length (m), root fresh weight (n), and shoot fresh weight (o) for plants grown in control nutrient solution and 20% PEG as in (k). n = 16 plants per genotype and treatment, except for TL4 (l) and TL11 (m) under 20% PEG (n = 15 plants). (p, q) Infrared thermography imaging (p) and temperature of leaves (q) for cv. Fielder (WT) and transgenic plants under well-watered control and drought-stress conditions. n = 20 leaves. (r) Water loss from detached leaves of wild-type cv. Fielder (WT) and transgenic plants during continuous dehydration on a clean bench under normal room temperature. n = 5 biological replicates. Fielder (WT) and transgenic seedling leaves grown under well-watered control and drought-stress conditions. n = 200 stomata. (u) Stomatal aperture between wild-type cv. Fielder (WT) and transgenic plants under well-watered control and drought-stress conditions. n = 200 stomata. Data are mean ± s.d. in (a), (c), (d), (f), (q), (r), and (u). Box plots in (h–j), (l–o), and (s) show the median (centre line), 25th–75th percentiles (box limits) and minimum and maximum values (whiskers), with individual data points overlaid. Statistical significance was determined by Brown–Forsythe and Welch ANOVA with two-sided Dunnett’s T3 test in (f), Kruskal–Wallis with two-sided Dunn’s test in (u), and one-way ANOVA with two-sided Dunnett’s multiple comparison test in remaining quantitative traits. *P < 0.05 and **P < 0.01 indicate statistically significant differences. Recent findings suggest that (a) Subcellular localization of GFP-fused EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ, and AtTFIIAγ. Wheat protoplasts were transformed with 35Spro:EpTFIIAγ–GFP, 35Spro:TaTFIIAγ–GFP, 35Spro:AtTFIIAγ–GFP, or 35Spro:GFP constructs. Green fluorescence signal was observed by confocal microscopy. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (4′,6-diamidino−2-phenylindole). Scale bar, 10 µm. (b) Western blot analysis using anti-GFP antibodies to determine whether fusion proteins are intact upon expression in wheat protoplasts as shown in (a). Actin was used as a loading control. (c) Yeast two-hybrid assay of physical interactions between the large (TFIIAαβ) and small subunits (TFIIAγ) of the TFIIA complex from wheat, Arabidopsis, and E. pusillum. BD–p53 and AD–SV40-T served as a positive control. (d) Luciferase complementation imaging of physical interactions between TFIIAαβ and TFIIAγ from wheat (top) and Arabidopsis (bottom). (e, f) In vitro pull-down assays of interactions between TFIIAαβ and TFIIAγ from wheat (e) and Arabidopsis (f). MBP–TFIIAγ was immobilized on Dextrin Beads 6FF and incubated with GST–TFIIAαβ. Immunoprecipitated fractions were probed by immunoblotting using anti-GST and anti-MBP antibodies. (g) Model of the transcription-initiation complex. A, B, D, and F represent TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID, and TFIIF, respectively. γ denotes the small subunit TFIIAγ, αβ represent the large subunit TFIIAαβ, TBP is the TATA-box-binding protein, and TAFs are TBP-associated factors. (h) EMSA of MBP–EpTFIIAγ and MBP–AtTFIIAγ binding to the TATA-box-containing element. (i) EMSA of MBP–EpTFIIAγ and MBP–TaTFIIAγ binding to the TATA-box-containing element. Decimals refer to the amount of protein loaded (in μg) per lane. (j) EMSA of full-length 6× His–EpTFIIAγ, the IDR-deletion variant (6× His–EpTFIIAγ/ΔIDR), IDR-fused 6× His–AtTFIIAγ and 6× His–TaTFIIAγ binding to the TATA-box-containing element. (k) Western blots of EpTFIIAγ/ΔIDR–HA expression in wild-type cv. Fielder and transgenic lines. Actin was used as a loading control. (l, m) Drought-tolerance phenotype (l) and survival rate (m) of wild-type and EpTFIIAγ/ΔIDR–HA lines. Photographs were taken before drought and after a post-drought 3-d re-watering period. Scale bars, 5 cm. n = 3 independent experiments. Data are mean ± s.d. Statistical significance was determined by Brown–Forsythe and Welch ANOVA with two-sided Dunnett’s T3 test was used in (m). Experiments were independently repeated three times with similar results in (a), (b), (e), and (f). Gel source data are shown in Supplementary Fig. 25.

(a) Functional co-expression network of EpTFIIAγ target genes. Co-expression relationships among EpTFIIAγ target genes were inferred from published expression data (https://wheat.cau.edu.cn/wGRN/) using the WGCNA signed topological overlap matrix (TOM). Node color denotes functional module, and larger nodes indicate EMSA-validated targets. (b, c) Volcano plots showing up-regulated and down-regulated genes in transgenic EpTFIIAγ line 4 (b) and line 7 (c) versus wild-type Fielder under well-watered conditions. Transcripts with a fold change > 2 or < 0.5 and an adjusted P-value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. (d, e) Venn diagram of up-regulated (d) and down-regulated (e) differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in two transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines compared to Fielder controls (|Fold Change| > 2, P < 0.05). (f, g) Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of up-regulated (f) and down-regulated (g) genes identified in transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines. In (b-e), statistical analysis of differentially expressed genes was conducted using the two-sided Wald test within the DESeq2 R package, with subsequent adjustment for multiple comparisons achieved through the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method. In (f) and (g), statistical analysis was assessed using a one-sided hypergeometric over-representation test.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Former Manchester United star Gordon Strachan - speaking exclusively to Sports Mole - has urged the Red Devils to sign a £62.8m midfielder to help correct their "phenomenal" transfer mistakes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 26 Nov 2026 10:16.

Former Manchester United star Gordon Strachan - speaking exclusively to Sports Mole - has urged the Red Devils to sign a £62.8m midfielder to help correct their "phenomenal" transfer mistakes.

Fresh Man Utd manager Mauricio Pochettino remains winless since replacing Michael Carrick following Wednesday's infuriating 2-2 draw with Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League, in which the Red Devils fell behind, took the lead and were then pegged back in Portugal.

The four-goal stalemate marked the seventh game in a row that Man United had conceded at least two goals, and once again, the Red Devils' open midfield was exposed.

The pairing of Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo did not cover themselves in glory against Liverpool or Sporting, and the former is now suspended for RB Leipzig in December after being sent off towards the end of Wednesday's game.

Andrey Santos has also not yet had the desired impact since joining from Chelsea, while fellow 22-year-old Carlos Baleba has played just 397 minutes across seven appearances due to injury problems.

Speaking to Sports Mole via William Hill betting site, Strachan - who scored 36 goals in 198 games for Man United - has told the Red Devils hierarchy to make a move for Crystal Palace lynchpin Adam Wharton to help offset the "phenomenal" amount of money the club has wasted on under-performing players.

It has been revealed that "Adam Wharton is one of my picks," Strachan mentioned. "Elliot Anderson was also another one they should have gone for. Tielemans has been doing well in the Premier League for nearly 10 years, so they're buying somebody who's at the latter stage of his career. I might be wrong, I hope I'm wrong, and hopefully, he’s got another five or six years in him.

According to recent reports, "And I've got to say, the world of football in England is full of the top teams, especially Chelsea, Spurs, bringing in players who sign for £40m, £50m, you go, who is he? There's just so many players like this now.

"You see some of these players, and you go, what has he done to deserve a £45m fee? Baleba, Santos, you’re picking up people for big fees, who have no reputation.

"Who's been brave here? Is this just a kind of cosy midfield? You could go back to Mason Mount for £40m - who actually signed this off to pay this amount of money for players?

"It’s just beyond belief the money that Man United have wasted. It's phenomenal. And that's from the recruitment not doing their work properly.

Recent findings suggest that "They've got to start saying, what is my plan for the next 10 years at Man United? And how do we go about this? Arsenal were a bit like that five or six years ago. It wasn't anywhere near as bad a situation as Man United, but they stuck to their plan, and it paid off.".

Data from the 2026-27 season does not paint Wharton in the most positive light compared to his Man United peers, given Crystal Palace's atrocious start to the campaign.

Indeed, the England international only leads Baleba, Tielemans, Santos and Mainoo on games played, crosses per 90 and accurate crosses per 90, while also winning the fewest duels and registering the lowest percentage of successful passes.

However, Wharton has committed the fewest fouls per 90 minutes of the quintet, and he has been dispossessed on the second-fewest occasions per 90 minutes, only behind Santos.

Thanks to Crystal Palace's perilous position in the Premier League table - Thomas Frank's men sit bottom of the rankings with just seven points from nine games - interested parties could pick up Wharton for a discount if the Eagles are relegated to the Championship.

The 22-year-old is valued at €75m (£62.8m) by Transfermarkt and has three years left on his Palace contract, but Man United may have to fend off competition from Liverpool and Chelsea to land him in 2027.

Gordon Strachan was speaking to Sports Mole on behalf of William Hill Football Odds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham United captain Jarrod Bowen has dismissed suggestions that the Hammers’ struggles to adapt to Championship football can be used as an excuse for their poor performances.
  • Industry observers note that the West Ham skipper remains confident that the club can secure promotion back to the Premier League, despite the Hammers having slipped to 13th in the Championship.
  • When asked about the difficulties of adapting to the Championship, Bowen said: “We can’t lean on that too much, we just have to face up to the facts that we haven’t been good enough.” The Hammers captain also touched upon his playing position during the interview, which was arguably one of the more interesting aspects of the discussion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United captain Jarrod Bowen has dismissed suggestions that the Hammers’ struggles to adapt to Championship football can be used as an excuse for their poor performances. Speaking to talkSPORT last night, Bowen acknowledged that the players simply haven’t been good enough.

Industry observers note that the West Ham skipper remains confident that the club can secure promotion back to the Premier League, despite the Hammers having slipped to 13th in the Championship. With second-placed Stoke City visiting the London Stadium on Saturday, Scott Parker is still searching for his first victory as head coach.

When asked about the difficulties of adapting to the Championship, Bowen said: “We can’t lean on that too much, we just have to face up to the facts that we haven’t been good enough.” The Hammers captain also touched upon his playing position during the interview, which was arguably one of the more interesting aspects of the discussion.

I’m pleased that Jarrod Bowen remarked West Ham haven’t been good enough, but having listened to the talkSPORT interview, I couldn’t help but think that he was trotting out what was expected of him. Understandably, the line of questioning was rather generic.

Personally, I’d have liked to know why Bowen has been stuck out on the wing and been so ineffective for much of the last three games. The Hammers skipper alluded to the fact that he’d not discussed his position with Parker, which I find astounding considering the influence Bowen had in a free role against Cardiff City.

As for the West Ham captaincy, well, the less mentioned about that the better. As Portsmouth went 1-0 up on Tuesday night, a distraught Fin Herrick lay on the ground beating his fist in frustration. He’s a rookie keeper who, in my opinion, had made another mistake and needed guidance.

What did Bowen do? Despite standing next to Herrick, Bowen turned on his heels, dropped his head and walked away, leaving the academy prospect to pick himself up and deal with it. Unacceptable.

Recent findings suggest that ideally, I’d have preferred a tougher line of questioning, drilling down into the specifics of exactly what is going on with West Ham’s best player. Instead, we got clichéd responses and a pledge that we’ll be involved in the promotion shake-up in May.

According to recent reports, AC Milan are not just looking for a upcoming source of goals in January. They are also searching for ways to help create them and keep them out.

Industry observers note that as Calciomercato.com report, Gerry Cardinale is determined to refine Ruben Amorim’s squad, which needs more quality and depth. Endrick remains the headline name that Milan are pursuing, but the idea of signing a left-back is gaining momentum quickly.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Sources indicate that while waiting for the arrival of Markus Krösche to be made official, work is already underway to examine the possibility of signing a latest defender. The very likely departure of Pervis Estupinan – who has suitors in Spain – could help facilitate a winter swoop for a left-sided player.

According to recent reports, noussair Mazraoui is one option, whose contract with Manchester United expires in 2028. It’s too early to know whether he’ll be a valuable asset to upcoming manager Mauricio Pochettino, but Amorim is an admirer of his and the Moroccan could be a versatile and experienced asset.

Another player whose contract expires in a year and a half is Alejandro Balde, whom Barcelona are looking to sell in January after unsuccessful attempts over the summer. His agent Jorge Mendes has offered him to several clubs, including Milan.

According to recent reports, the directors are keeping him on their list. This year, he’s made just five appearances for a total of 125 minutes across LaLiga and the Champions League. So, he might have to leave the Blaugrana to play more regularly.

There are a couple of domestic options too. Gabriele Calvani is shining for Frosinone (though he struggled on Sunday in his San Siro audition). The 22-year-old centre-back can play full-back, and while he is owned by Genoa, the two clubs are in talks over Christian Comotto which could aid things.

In a recent development, juan Miranda is the other name, even though he is negotiating a contract renewal with Bologna given his deal expires in 2028. The Spaniard is an old favourite having been linked before, and he would be expected to cost €15m or more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 08:22 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:10 EST, 25 November 2026.

A smile did eventually spread across the face of Erling Haaland when dissecting Manchester City’s draw with Napoli, stretching their worrying run to one victory in five games.

Sources indicate that not for the first time in recent weeks, he had appeared morose and despondent, radiating an air of gloom, talking about how the team are ‘questioning anything’ amid these results. That’s not exactly inspiring confidence among their supporters.

According to recent reports, but just as City’s captain for the night was about to finish his media duties before heading home, one final question focused on Sunday’s clash with Arsenal and a rivalry with a ‘certain centre half’. Haaland’s mood changed instantly.

‘It's always good to play against the best teams,’ said the Norwegian, breaking out into a smirk as he allowed the impending battle with Gabriel to percolate.

‘Arsenal were the best team last year and one of the best in the last five years now, so it's fun to play against them and it’s always fun to play against Gabriel.’.

In a recent development, there was, at last, some positive emotion. Is Gabriel and that playground scrapping what he needs to re-energise? We’ll find out in a few days.

Erling Haaland appeared morose and despondent following Man City's draw with Napoli, suggesting he was 'questioning everything' amid their worrying run of form.

Haaland did raise a smile about the prospect of his impending battle with Arsenal defender Gabriel this weekend.

The Man City star has shown increasing dejected body language during games and has spent too much time recently with his head bowed and hand waving at team-mates.

Haaland talked about City needing to be at their maximum to take anything from the Emirates this weekend. Whether that is ‘fun’ or not is a different matter entirely, but what Enzo Maresca must demand more from all of his players. Even with 14 goals already this term, that includes Haaland.

He is leading from the front off the pitch. Standing in front of the cameras more than anyone else, facing up to the dipping form and taking on those responsibilities without complaining. The forward wrote on X on Wednesday afternoon: 'Together through the ups and downs. Thank you for pushing us until the very end yesterday. Full focus on Sunday now.'.

Yet City need more of that leadership between the white lines from somebody who has drawn a blank in four of his last five club matches, despite scoring three times over the international break.

There is too much head bowing and hand waving at the moment.

According to recent reports, the 26-year-old admits he has to give extra. And believes that the team are generally creating enough chances for him, even if the freewheeling attacking abandon of early season has vanished.

City's results are clearly affecting Haaland’s mood and that can be self-perpetuating. He admits that failing to reverse this run is hurting him. That is evident by watching his increasingly dejected body language during games and the frustration seen when he gestured at Abdukodir Khusanov as the defender dithered with a routine throw-in during Saturday’s draw against Fulham. It wasn’t the picture of a man happy with his lot.

Only Haaland will know whether that general angst is contributing to a lack of intensity in his own performances. Nobody has mentioned the striker carrying a knock, although Maresca has appeared focused on offering him rest whenever possible over the past three months.

In a recent development, something is undoubtedly proving an obstacle for him. He’s insisted that it isn’t the guilty verdicts hanging over City and, listening to him, the gripes and disappointment look focused on City’s lack of control in games. It also cannot help that Haaland will feel aggrieved to have seen a goal on Saturday chalked off for a foul on Bernd Leno and then to have not been awarded a penalty for grappling on Tuesday night.

If both or even one of those decisions go his way, the interview that sparked concern with fans – one conducted almost immediately after full time when emotions are at their highest – would likely have been very different.

City will have to cling on to the idea that a sullen Haaland is at least a Haaland who cares. And a Haaland who cares must surely dig them out of this hole, even if he cannot do that alone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 10:27.

Bournemouth have prepared for their Europa League clash at Celta Vigo in the knowledge that they could smash even more history.

Marco Rose's side won just two of their opening eight competitive matches of the 2026-27 season, hinting that there could be a period of struggle following Andoni Iraola's departure to Liverpool.

However, with the Cherries set for a Celta Vigo challenge on Thursday night, it is clear that the Dean Court club are thriving, with the visitors to Spain sitting in fifth position in the Premier League standings.

A star of the current positive form, Evanilson has truly unveiled himself as an elite top-flight striker, netting seven goals and providing two assists in his past eight appearances, scoring in five consecutive league fixtures.

What makes Bournemouth's run even more impressive is that last season's star man Junior Kroupi has barely started a competitive match so far after recovering from a broken leg sustained over the summer.

Starting with a 3-0 Europa League success over Austrian side Sturm Graz on October 15, Bournemouth have recorded nine straight victories in all competitions across the Premier League, EFL Cup and European action.

That winning streak is the longest since the Cherries became a Football League club at the beginning of the 1923-24 season, showcasing how impressively the South Coast team are performing at the moment.

However, there are still more records to be achieved over the coming weeks, with Bournemouth aiming to become only the eighth team to record 10 straight competitive victories whilst playing in the Premier League.

Winning the Premier League during the 2016-17 campaign under Antonio Conte, Chelsea managed 10 wins in a row in all competitions, with that particular streak running from October 2016 until New Year's Eve 2016.

Leeds are the other club to post that exact number of wins in succession, with the Elland Road side completing the feat between August and October during the 1999-00 Premier League term.

The dominant force in English domestic football during the late 2010s and early 2020s, Manchester City are unsurprisingly the club with the most consecutive competitive wins as a Premier League side.

Under the expert stewardship of Pep Guardiola, the title-winning Citizens won 21 straight matches between December 2020 and March 2021, destroying Arsenal's previous record of 13 games in succession.

To match Man City's record, Bournemouth would need to secure victory in Spain on Thursday before winning every single match up to and including the trip to Brighton & Hove Albion on January 5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

It has been revealed that the veteran captain mentioned: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

FC Midtjylland winger Mikel Gogorza has confirmed that West Ham United submitted a concrete transfer offer for him during the summer window. The 20-year-old has also revealed that playing in England remains his dream, despite rejecting the opportunity to join the Hammers.

Speaking to Danish publication Bold following Midtjylland’s 2-0 Conference League victory over Pafos last night, Gogorza explained that the offer arrived whilst he was recovering from a groin injury. According to an English translation of the interview published by Sport Witness, West Ham’s bid was worth approximately £12 million.

Gogorza revealed that both he and his club felt it was key for him to spend another season in Denmark following his injury. With the January transfer window approaching and Scott Parker’s team struggling for attacking inspiration, it’ll be interesting to see whether the Hammers revisit any of their summer transfer targets.

I’d certainly be hoping that West Ham wouldn’t be revisiting their interest in Gogorza, primarily because I don’t believe him to be an upgrade on what we have. He certainly doesn’t appear to be worth a £18 million gamble which is the number at the moment being quoted.

Sources indicate that look, the jury is still out on Edvin Austbø, who appears to be a promising player. But I’m firmly of the opinion that West Ham do need another winger, ideally one who’s versatile enough to play on both sides.

It would be my preference to have somebody with experience of English football, and I’m intrigued to find out where Nils Koppen has been focusing his interest.

It’s worth remembering that last summer, as Claret & Hugh exclusively revealed at the time, the Hammers hierarchy hired Ben Chorley to assist with identifying Championship-based players.

💡 Key Takeaways
